newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU agrees labelling rules for novel foods.
newsitem.headline: EU agrees labelling rules for novel foods.

text.p: European Union states and the European Parliament have agreed labelling rules for novel foods containing genetically modified organisms (GMOs), the Irish EU Presidency said in a statement on Thursday.

"The agreement reached represented an equitable balance which would provide consumers with the assurances they require while at the same time facilitating the development needs of the food industry," said Jimmy Deenihan, Irish junior farm minister.
EU governments wanted to label only novel foods which were significantly different from conventional foods while the parliament wanted much stricter rules.
Under the agreement, reached after several weeks of talks under the so-called conciliation procedure, labelling will only be needed on foods containing "live" genetically modified cells.

Food made from GMOs but not containing "live" modified cells would have to be labelled if it differed from conventional food beyond "accepted limits of natural variation", or if it caused special nutritional or ethical concern for consumers.
This means that soyoil, used in cooking and salads, and tomato paste which may contain modified organisms but do not contain "live" modified cells will not have to carry special labels.

"Each time that you can detect a difference, you have to label the product. The more intensive the processing the more difficult it is to prove that the original product was genetically altered," an EU diplomat explained.
German socialist members of the parliament, who had insisted that consumers should be fully informed about what they are eating, welcomed the compromise.
"We have reached the best possible agreement. I am confident that European consumers will be safeguarded," German Social Democrat Dagmar Roth-Behrendt said in a statement.
But ecologist members were dissatisfied. "There are too many escape clauses, too few safety guarantees and too much potential for manipulation of the system," the Greens Group said in a statement.
